claim: The Java Virtual Machine Specification does not mandate any internal structure for objects, so header size, header contents and field order are all implementation choices.
note: This is the one JVMS claim in the lesson, and it is the claim that makes every other claim here a HOTSPOT claim. Worth checking carefully in review.

claim: With UseCompactObjectHeaders on, the object header is 8 bytes and the compressed class pointer lives in bits 63 to 42 of the mark word.
measured: first field offset is 8 for OneInt, OneRef, Integer, Long and Two, on osx-arm64 and linux-x64, build 27+35-2325

claim: With UseCompactObjectHeaders off, the header is 12 bytes: an 8 byte mark word followed by a separate 4 byte class pointer.
measured: first field offset is 12 for Two, OneRef and Integer under -XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders, on both machines

claim: UseCompactObjectHeaders is on by default on 64 bit platforms from JDK 27.
measured: the banner reports UseCompactObjectHeaders true with origin default

claim: Instance size is the end of the last field rounded up to ObjectAlignmentInBytes, which defaults to 8, so a 4 byte reduction in header size does not imply a 4 byte reduction in object size.
measured: java.lang.Integer is 16 bytes both ways: 8+4 padded to 16, and 12+4 exactly 16
note: This is the claim the whole lesson exists for and the one gate 3 tests. The citation used to point at the layout comment in markWord.hpp rather than at the alignment code, and it now points at align_object_size, which is the rounding itself. The default of 8 is src/hotspot/share/runtime/globals.hpp:134@jdk-27+35, one line below the UseCompactObjectHeaders default that O01-C4 cites.

claim: The bottom two bits of the mark word are the lock state, and 01 means unlocked.
measured: every mark word read in this lesson ends in 01 unless something is holding a lock

claim: The identity hash occupies bits 41 to 11 of the mark word and is written the first time anything asks for it, not at allocation.
measured: the word is 0 in that range before System.identityHashCode and equals the returned hash after

claim: The age field counts collections survived and is live state, so a freshly allocated object can already read a nonzero age if a young collection happened between the allocation and the read.
measured: the first jvx.freshMark of a kernel reports age 1 and the collection count goes 0 to 1 across that call, every later call reports age 0

claim: The value in the klass bits is an offset into the class metadata region, so it depends on load order and is not comparable between runs or machines.
measured: Object read 0x0017ac on osx-arm64 and 0x001774 on linux-x64, same build, while two instances of the same class always agree

claim: Assigning an object to a top level JShell variable causes its identity hash to be written, so an object observed across two cells is not in its allocated state.
measured: on 27+35-2325 osx-arm64, an object assigned to a top level variable reads a nonzero hash even when the line ends in a semicolon, the same allocation stored into a static field of a class declared in the same session reads 0, and one that is never named reads 0. Reading the mark word is not itself enough to write one. Two runs, different hashes, same three answers
note: This is a JShell property rather than a HotSpot one, and the marker is on the header field it disturbs rather than on the cause. The control is the static field: it proves the cause is the top level variable and not the allocation, and it rules out the reading. Revisit when the JShell distortion report in issue #2 is finished, because the cause deserves its own citation into the JShell sources.
